findings.passage: He chose a field by asking where he "could be best in the world."
findings.problem: This misstates the source, and it leads the Three-over-One discriminator. In Stratechery (S28, reopened 2026-10-07, Background section), "best in the world" was the bar he set for doubling down on any field. The choice between acting and science turned on impact: "I ended up picking the hard sciences one, because I felt like maybe that was an area where I could most make a difference in the world." The article says this correctly earlier ("his bar for committing to a field was being best in the world, though the choice itself turned on impact"). This sentence contradicts that and brings back the misreading that critic-05 had fixed, now in the most load-bearing paragraph. C04's claim text has the same blend.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence describes "best in the world" as the bar he set for committing to a field, not the question that picked it. Example: He set his bar for any field at being able to "be best in the world." It matches the earlier section. No body, FAQ or evidence text (C04 claim, C184) says he chose a field by where he could be best.

findings.passage: His moral vocabulary turns up most when he judges others.
findings.problem: The discriminator sets aside the One reading's strongest private evidence by misfiling it. Two of the moral items the article itself quotes do not judge other people. The 2017 diary rule "cannot say that we are committed to the non-profit . . . if three months later we're doing b-corp then it was a lie" (New Yorker, S23, reopened) and the November 2017 entry "it'd be wrong to steal the nonprofit from him. to convert to a b-corp without him. that'd be pretty morally bankrupt" (MIT Technology Review, S27, reopened) both judge what he and his co-founders were considering doing. Both sit in a private diary with no audience. They are first-person rightness-scoring of his own conduct, the very kind of self-report the next sentence calls "the better test." The evidence record's discriminator lists "Musk" among the others judged, which misdescribes the entry. As written, the reader cannot see that the Three lead holds only for how he scores his work, not his conduct.
findings.acceptance_test: The discriminator paragraph, C184 and type_hypothesis.discriminator state the split accurately. For example: his moral vocabulary appears when he judges conduct, including his own planned conduct in the 2017 diary, while his accounts of his own work score it by rank, notice and results. One or two sentences say why the self-directed diary entries do not overturn the Three lead, or the confidence wording drops. The "Why isn't Greg Brockman a Type 1?" FAQ stays consistent. The body stays at or under 4,500 words (it is 4,464 now); trim elsewhere if needed.

findings.passage: and this was the first of two times he set it aside with nothing to show.
findings.problem: The 2016 essay (S03, reopened) says he "managed to build something that could talk about the weather very convincingly" before finding that "no one had any techniques that could make my bot really work." He then shelved it and "decided to focus on creating systems that can have a real impact." The 2026 telling (S28), quoted in this same paragraph, describes a chatbot game with 1,500 users in a day and "the most glorious feeling." "Nothing to show" contradicts both. It also stretches the thesis phrase from the Dota essay into a recurrence the sources do not support (C143 is unsupported as worded). The "real impact" pivot that fan-04's acceptance test required is still missing.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence describes the gap-year shelving in his terms: the bot could not be made to "really work," and he turned to systems with "a real impact." It is dated and linked to the 2016 essay, and it no longer says he had "nothing to show." If the "two times" recurrence stays, it is framed as setting AI aside when he could not make it work. C143's claim and passage match the new wording.

findings.passage: The Wall Street Journal's account of the OpenAI–Anthropic rift, by Keach Hagey and Berber Jin and largely from unnamed sources, begins with 2017 layoffs
findings.problem: The WSJ account (S22, To Vima syndication, reopened) begins in 2016 at the Delano Avenue group house, with Brockman's debate with Dario Amodei and Holden Karnofsky. The 2017 layoffs come later, in its "Early traumas" section. "Begins with" is inaccurate.
findings.acceptance_test: "Begins with" is replaced by an accurate verb, such as "reports" or "traces the friction to." The paragraph is otherwise unchanged.

findings.passage: "I didn't feel confident in my work, but to make it worse, other people did,"
findings.problem: Two direct quotations are verified correct but missing from the claim inventory: this hook quote (S06, "Dota" section) and "circling" in the closing paragraph (S24, about 0:22:47). The standard asks for every direct quote to be inventoried. Separately, C60's claim text says "Hedley" where the source says Hedlund.
findings.acceptance_test: The evidence record has a claim, or an extended passage on an existing claim, for the hook quote (S06) and for "circling" (S24). C60's claim text says Hedlund. No article text changes.

findings.passage: Like I just like run right in.
findings.problem: The closing quote rests on speech recognition only. I transcribed the original podcast audio (megaphone episode, about 22:10-22:45) with Whisper medium.en and large-v3-turbo. Both confirm every content word: "in the trenches kind of leader," "lead from the front," "getting a little emotional," "look back to see if everyone's following," "just like run right in." They differ from the YouTube auto-captions only on fillers. Medium.en has no "Sorry" or "Um" and gives "right, just like run right in." Large-v3-turbo gives "I just like run right in." Whisper tends to drop disfluencies, so the caption version is probably the verbatim one, but no one has listened to it.
findings.acceptance_test: Before publication, someone listens at about 0:22:11-0:22:29 (YouTube) and confirms "Sorry," "Um," and "Like I just like run right in." Otherwise, the quote drops only the unconfirmed filler words and marks the omissions with ellipses, keeping "I'm getting a little emotional" and "just like run right in."
